To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we derived an exposure-response relationship (ERC) for diesel engine exhaust (DE) and lung cancer mortality using a meta-regression approach and that we estimated excess lifetime risks (ELRs), based on the derived ERC, for several exposure scenarios.

the combined data from the three U.S. studies indicate that the lifetime risk of dying of lung cancer due to occupational exposure to diesel exhaust at levels common in trucking is 200/10,000, and the risk of death from lung cancer in the general population from environmental exposures to diesel exhaust at current levels is 21/10,000.

We derived an exposure-response curve (ERC) based on meta-analysis of data from three large occupational cohort study and used it to estimate excess lung cancer risks from diesel engine exhaust (DE) exposure in the general population.

the health effects of diesel exhaust exposure, which has recently been classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as “carcinogenic to humans.”
the effects of diesel exhaust on lung cancer.
the development of an exposure-response function for the carcinogenicity of DEE, which is based on data from large occupational cohorts.

we found evidence of an association between DEE exposure and lung cancer mortality in occupational studies, and based on these data, we estimated that DEE exposure may cause 1–2% of all lung cancer deaths in the United States.
diesel exhaust is a lung cancer risk factor.

The main takeaway from our work is that

diesel exhaust is a potent human carcinogen, with a lifetime excess risk of lung cancer mortality of 1/10,000 for occupational exposure at 1 µg/m3 elemental carbon (EC) (a proxy for diesel exhaust) and 1/10 for lifetime exposure to the outdoor air concentration in the U.S. in the 1980s (approximately 0.8 µg/m3 EC).
there are substantial risks of lung cancer from occupational and environmental exposure to diesel exhaust.
